name: Latanoprost

card.summary: A glaucoma eye drop whose lash-lengthening and eye-darkening side effects get it mentioned in appearance circles; no cosmetic trials exist.
card.note: Iris darkening is listed as likely permanent on the label; not approved for cosmetic use.

quick.overview:
Latanoprost is a prescription eye drop for glaucoma and raised eye pressure. Its label lists longer, thicker, darker eyelashes and darker eyelid skin and irises among its effects.

Looksmaxxing discussion is sparse and mostly about eye darkening. No trial has tested it for cosmetic purposes; a Phase 1/2 trial pairing it with laser in alopecia areata is registered.
quick.mechanism: It is a prostaglandin F2-alpha analogue that increases fluid drainage from the eye through the uveoscleral pathway, lowering pressure. Pigment and lash changes are tissue effects of the same drug class.
quick.risks: Label warnings include permanent iris pigmentation, eyelid darkening, inflammation and macular oedema. A case report describes skin depigmentation. It is prescription-only and not approved for cosmetic use.

lead: Latanoprost is a synthetic prostaglandin F2-alpha analogue applied as an ophthalmic solution to lower raised intraocular pressure (IOP) in open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension. The US label describes its main action as increasing uveoscleral outflow of aqueous humour.[1][2] It is a prescription medicine, and its approved use is medical rather than cosmetic.

Its relevance to appearance comes from effects listed on its label: increased length, thickness, pigmentation and number of eyelashes, darkening of eyelid skin, and permanent darkening of the iris.[1] Wikipedia notes latanoprost has also been used cosmetically to lengthen and thicken lashes, and the related prostaglandin analogue bimatoprost is marketed for eyelash growth.[24][25] A looksmax.org thread discusses prostaglandin drops as a way to darken eye colour.[11]

Latanoprost is also under development as a topical hair-growth agent: Wikipedia reports Phase 1b/2a topline results in July 2024 for latanoprost-based products for androgenetic alopecia, and a registered Phase 1/2 trial lists it with fractional laser for alopecia areata.[24][3] No published trial tests latanoprost as a cosmetic eyelash or eye-colour treatment; evidence for its lash effect comes from glaucoma trials and the label.

chain: FP-receptor agonist acts on lash follicles and iris melanocytes
Lashes lengthen and thicken; iris pigment can increase
Fuller lashes, darker iris (permanent for the iris per the label)
angle.text: Longer, thicker, darker eyelashes are a labelled effect of latanoprost, and iris darkening is described as likely permanent. People in appearance communities mention it mostly for the eye-colour effect, while lash growth is the better-known prostaglandin-analogue effect.

infobox: Raised intraocular pressure in open-angle glaucoma / ocular hypertension[1]
Pfizer; Xalatan now marketed by Viatris[24]
Prescription-only (US, UK, EU, Australia); generics available[24]

paras: The US label indicates latanoprost 0.005% for reducing elevated IOP in patients with open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension.[1] Early six-month randomised trials compared once-daily latanoprost with twice-daily timolol in several countries and found it lowered pressure at least as well, with the advantage of once-daily use.[4][5][6] Wikipedia summarises pressure reductions of 22 to 39 percent over one to twelve months and notes it beat timolol in three of four large trials.[24] A meta-analysis of randomised trials of common glaucoma drugs and a later network meta-analysis of first-line agents both include prostaglandin analogues among the most effective topical options.[7][8] The UK Glaucoma Treatment Study, a placebo-controlled trial, reported visual-field preservation with latanoprost in newly diagnosed open-angle glaucoma.[9]

Eyelash lengthening and thickening is a recognised effect of latanoprost and other prostaglandin analogues; the label states the changes are usually reversible.[1] Wikipedia notes that latanoprost is also used cosmetically for lash growth, while its sister drug bimatoprost is the prostaglandin analogue that has a dedicated eyelash product.[24][25] Eyelash growth has also been noted as a common mild adverse event of travoprost.[10] Latanoprost itself is not approved for eyelash enhancement.

A looksmax.org thread discusses latanoprost, bimatoprost and travoprost as agents that can darken eye colour; its author described the idea as of limited usefulness and risky because the drugs are glaucoma treatments, and asked that it not be taken too seriously.[11] The label states that iris pigmentation is likely to be permanent.[1]

The US label lists iris pigmentation changes, eyelid skin darkening, eyelash changes, intraocular inflammation (iritis/uveitis) and macular oedema, including cystoid macular oedema, among reported reactions. It says pigmentation can increase for as long as treatment continues, and that iris pigmentation is likely to be permanent while eyelash changes are usually reversible.[1] Wikipedia lists blurred vision, stinging, eye redness, itching and brown iris pigmentation as common (over 5 percent), eyelid crusting and swelling in 1 to 4 percent, and iritis, uveitis and retinal detachment as rare.[24] Grokipedia adds that iris changes are more pronounced in people with mixed-colour irises.[12]

A published case report describes skin depigmentation associated with latanoprost use.[13] Wikipedia reports research suggesting that wiping excess fluid from the eye after instillation is linked to less eyelash shortening and eyelid hyperpigmentation.[24][25] The label notes that no adequate well-controlled studies exist in pregnant women and that animal studies using intravenous dosing showed malformations and embryofetal loss.[1]

Latanoprost is an ester prodrug converted to latanoprost acid, a selective agonist at the prostaglandin F receptor. The label says its main mechanism, from animal and human studies, is increased uveoscleral outflow of aqueous humour.[1][24] Onset is about three to four hours, with peak effect at 8 to 12 hours and a duration of at least 24 hours; it degrades with heat and ultraviolet light.[24] Reviews of prostaglandin mechanisms describe tissue remodelling in the outflow pathways as part of the effect.[2][14] Small clinical studies have also measured effects on choroidal thickness.[15][16]

Phase 3 programmes ran in Scandinavia, the United Kingdom and the US from late 1992 through the mid-1990s, comparing latanoprost with timolol.[26][27][23] It was approved for medical use in the US and EU in 1996 and is described as the first prostaglandin analogue for glaucoma.[24][12] Pfizer developed it; after Pfizer's Upjohn unit combined with Mylan, Xalatan is marketed by Viatris, and later formulations such as Iyuzeh, Xelpros and Catiolanze followed, the last recommended by the EMA in 2023.[24] It is on the WHO Essential Medicines List and is available as a generic.[24]

Wikipedia reports that latanoprost is being developed as a topical treatment for androgenic alopecia alone and in combinations with minoxidil and with minoxidil plus finasteride, with Dermaliq Therapeutics announcing positive Phase 1b/2a topline results in July 2024.[24] A systematic review of androgenetic alopecia treatments does not establish latanoprost as a treatment in that condition.[22]

Human studies are overwhelmingly in glaucoma and ocular hypertension. Large randomised trials from the 1990s (US, Scandinavian and UK groups) compared latanoprost with timolol over six months,[4][5][6] and a two-year analysis and a one-year combination trial with timolol followed.[17][18] Head-to-head trials compared it with bimatoprost and travoprost.[19][20][21]

No published trial of latanoprost for cosmetic eyelash enhancement or eye-colour change was identified. The one registered trial related to hair is a Phase 1/2 study (n=70, start 2024, status unknown) of latanoprost combined with fractional erbium-YAG laser in alopecia areata.[3]

Latanoprost is a prescription medicine in the US, UK, EU and Australia.[24] In looksmaxxing forums it appears mainly in passing, as a drug whose documented effects touch on eye colour and lashes; the one thread in this area frames it as a curiosity rather than a protocol, and replies joked about eye colour preferences.[11]

lore.intro: Latanoprost is a minor topic in appearance communities, mentioned chiefly for its eye-darkening side effect.[11]

claims.claim: Prostaglandin drops such as latanoprost can make eyes darker
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster, studying pharmacology, noted that these drops can change eye colour and raised it as a possibility for people wanting darker eyes, while calling it risky.[11]
claims.experts: The US label lists iris pigmentation increase as a warning and says it is likely permanent.[1]

claims.believers: Users discussing prostaglandin analogues cite lash growth as a known effect.[11]
claims.experts: The label lists increased length, thickness, pigmentation and number of lashes, usually reversible; it is not approved for cosmetic use.[1]
